docs.title: GeoFlow Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the official documentation for GeoFlow (gf).

GeoFlow is a production-quality Python package that provides a Google Earth Engine-like developer experience (Image, ImageCollection, FeatureCollection, Filter, Reducer), while seamlessly integrating with the Python geospatial ecosystem (xarray, geopandas, scikit-learn).

It specifically introduces first-class features for Spatial Statistics, Leakage-Safe Spatial Machine Learning, and Publication Cartography.

docs.title: Contributor & Developer Guide
docs.text: Welcome to the GeoFlow contributor guide! This document explains GeoFlow's software architecture, engineering patterns, development setup, testing protocols, and known roadmap areas.

docs.title: 1. Architectural Philosophy
docs.text: GeoFlow is designed around three foundational principles: 1. Google Earth Engine (GEE) Familiarity: Provide the intuitive, chainable API that remote sensing researchers love (Image, ImageCollection, FeatureCollection, Filter, Reducer, Map.addLayer). 2. Native Python Execution: Execute computations locally using industry-standard Python libraries (NumPy, Rasterio, GeoPandas, SciPy, PySAL, PyTorch, Xarray) without requiring proprietary cloud runtimes. 3. Scientific Rigor: Treat spatial autocorrelation, pseudoreplication, and spatial ML data leakage as first-class architectural concerns rather than afterthoughts.

docs.title: Initializing Environment
docs.text:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/ramiz-moktader/geoflow.git
cd geoflow

# Create and activate a virtual environment
python -m venv .venv

# On Linux/macOS:
source .venv/bin/activate
# On Windows PowerShell:
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Install in editable mode with all optional dependencies
pip install -e ".[all]"

# Install documentation & testing tools
pip install pytest pytest-cov mkdocs-material

docs.title: The _clone() Pattern & Subclass Propagation
docs.text:
GeoFlow enables users to subclass Image, ImageCollection, or FeatureCollection to add domain methods. All internal operations (such as .select(), .add(), .ndvi(), .clip()) must preserve the custom subclass and its custom instance attributes:

# From geoflow/raster/image.py:
def _clone(self, data: np.ndarray, band_names: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> Any:
    names = band_names if band_names is not None else self._band_names
    new_obj = self.__class__(
        data,
        transform=self._transform,
        crs=self._crs,
        band_names=names,
        nodata=self._nodata,
        metadata=dict(self._metadata),
    )
    # Propagate custom subclass attributes
    for k, v in self.__dict__.items():
        if k not in ("_data", "_transform", "_crs", "_band_names", "_nodata", "_metadata"):
            new_obj.__dict__[k] = v
    return new_obj
When implementing new raster methods, always use self._clone(new_data, ...) rather than instantiating Image(...) directly.

docs.title: Strict CRS Awareness
docs.text: GeoFlow methods must never silently mix or corrupt Coordinate Reference Systems. - Use check_crs_compatibility(self.crs, other.crs, context="...") before binary raster math or geometric intersections. - When sampling rasters at point coordinates (e.g. fc.sample_raster(image)), reproject the coordinates to the image's coordinate space on-the-fly rather than reprojecting the entire raster grid.

docs.title: Fluent Functional Composition (.pipe())
docs.text:
All EarthObject instances support .pipe(func, *args, **kwargs): 

def mask_clouds(img, threshold=20):
    return img.updateMask(img.select("cloud_mask") < threshold)

processed = img.pipe(mask_clouds, threshold=15).pipe(calc_indices)

docs.title: 5. Testing Protocols
docs.text: GeoFlow uses pytest. All Matplotlib figures created during tests must be cleaned up to avoid resource leaks. conftest.py handles this automatically via the cleanup_figures fixture.

docs.title: Running Test Suites
docs.text:
# Run all tests
pytest -v

# Run with coverage report
pytest --cov=geoflow --cov-report=term-missing

# Run quick end-to-end integration test
python test_quick.py

docs.title: Adding New Tests
docs.text:
• Unit tests belong in dedicated test files prefixed with test_ at the repository root or in a tests/ directory.
  • Test both NumPy array inputs and rasterio-backed datasets.
  • Test that custom subclasses persist through your new method chain.

docs.title: 6. Known Limitations & Roadmap
docs.text:
Issues from the codebase audit have been fixed and are covered by test_audit_regressions.py. The following limitations remain; contributions are welcome:

Area Current Behavior Recommended Improvement Basemap terms of use The default HYBRID/TERRAIN basemaps load Google tiles directly, which Google's terms do not permit outside its APIs. Switch the default to an open basemap (e.g. Esri SATELLITE or OpenStreetMap) and keep Google as opt-in. login() verification Credentials from environment variables or ~/.netrc are reported as authenticated without contacting Earthdata. Validate with a lightweight authenticated request (e.g. URS profile endpoint). Variogram memory variogram() builds all point pairs: memory grows as $O(n^2)$. Subsample pairs or bin with a KD-tree for large point sets. LISA inference Local Moran's I uses analytical p-values without multiple-testing correction, so many clusters can be false positives. Add conditional permutation inference and FDR / Bonferroni correction. Spatial ESS effective_sample_size uses the AR(1) formula with Moran's I as $\rho$, a screening heuristic. Offer variogram- or model-based effective sample sizes. CRS hashing CRS defines __eq__ without __hash__, so CRS objects can't be used in sets or as dict keys. Implement __hash__ from the normalised WKT / EPSG code. Filter errors Filter.__call__ treats any exception inside a predicate as "no match". Raise or warn on predicate errors other than missing properties. focal_median with NaN Falls back to a slow generic_filter when the band contains NaN. Use a vectorized NaN-aware median filter. Map image overlays Rasters are reprojected to EPSG:4326 and drawn on Web Mercator, which stretches large extents in latitude. Reproject overlays to EPSG:3857 before rendering. Downloader filenames Files are named by the URL's last path segment; two granules with the same name overwrite each other. Namespace downloads by collection/granule ID.

docs.title: 7. Documentation Workflow
docs.text:
The documentation is generated using MkDocs with the Material theme:

# Serve documentation locally with live reload
mkdocs serve

# Build production static bundle
mkdocs build

When contributing code: 1. Update docstrings following Google / NumPy style. 2. Update the corresponding markdown file in docs/api_reference/. 3. Add tutorials or practical examples in docs/user_guide/ if introducing user-facing capabilities.

docs.title: 8. Pull Request Guidelines
docs.text:
1. Branch Naming: Use descriptive branch names (e.g. fix/image-comparison-operators, feat/modis-adapter, docs/api-overhaul).
  2. Clean Commits: Write clear, descriptive commit messages.
  3. Pass Tests: Ensure pytest passes with zero failures before opening a PR.
  4. Documentation: Any new feature or bug fix must include corresponding documentation and test coverage.
  5. Backwards Compatibility: Do not remove public methods from gf.__all__ without a deprecation warning cycle.

docs.title: CLI Reference (geoflow.cli)
docs.text: GeoFlow provides a command-line interface (geoflow) for querying NASA Earthdata granules, inspecting environment configurations, and checking hardware acceleration status without writing Python scripts.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
When GeoFlow is installed via pip, the geoflow CLI binary is automatically registered in your environment PATH:

geoflow --help

docs.title: geoflow search
docs.text:
Search NASA Earthdata Common Metadata Repository (CMR) directly from your terminal.

geoflow search DATASET [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: • DATASET: Target dataset name or alias (e.g. SENTINEL-2, LANDSAT-8, GEDI/L2A, MODIS).

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• --bbox TEXT: Geographic bounding box as minx,miny,maxx,maxy (e.g. 91.7,22.2,92.0,22.5).
  • --start TEXT: Start date formatted as YYYY-MM-DD.
  • --end TEXT: End date formatted as YYYY-MM-DD.
  • --limit INTEGER: Maximum number of granule records to return (default: 10).

docs.title: Example
docs.text: geoflow search SENTINEL-2 --bbox "91.7,22.2,92.0,22.5" --start "2023-01-01" --end "2023-01-15" --limit 5

docs.title: Core API Reference (geoflow.core)
docs.text:
The core package holds the building blocks shared by every other subsystem. Everything here is importable from geoflow.core; Filter, Reducer, CRS and reproject_bounds are also re-exported at the top level (gf.Filter, ...).

Symbol Kind Source EarthObject base class geoflow/core/base.py config singleton geoflow/core/config.py CRS class geoflow/core/crs.py reproject_bounds function geoflow/core/crs.py check_crs_compatibility function geoflow/core/crs.py Filter class geoflow/core/filter.py Reducer class geoflow/core/reducer.py

docs.title: EarthObject
docs.text:
EarthObject(metadata: dict | None = None)

Base class of Image, ImageCollection, Geometry, Feature, FeatureCollection and GEDI. It provides a metadata dictionary and a provenance log.

Member Signature Description metadata property → dict The live metadata dict (mutations are visible). get get(property_name, default=None) Read a metadata key. set set(property_name, value) -> self Write a metadata key in place and return self (unlike GEE, this mutates). track_action track_action(action_name, params=None) Append an entry to the provenance log. history property → list[dict] Copy of the provenance log. Starts with a "created" entry (UTC ISO timestamp). pipe pipe(func, *args, **kwargs) Returns func(self, *args, **kwargs), so custom steps can be chained fluently.

Note

Built-in operations do not call track_action yet, so history only contains the creation entry plus anything you add yourself.

img = gf.Image(arr).set("sensor", "S2A")
img.get("sensor")                     # "S2A"
img.pipe(lambda im, k: im * k, 2.0)   # same as img * 2.0

docs.title: config
docs.text:
Module-level singleton instance of Config. It is created at import time and creates ~/.geoflow/cache as a side effect.

Attribute Default Used by default_crs "EPSG:4326" Informational (CLI info). cache_dir ~/.geoflow/cache Informational. download_dir <cwd>/data Informational (downloaders take explicit output_dir). backend "auto" Informational ("auto", "cpu", "cuda", "mps"). workers 4 Informational. strict_crs False Not enforced yet. verbose True Not used yet. Method Description set_cache_dir(path) Set and create the cache directory. set_backend(name) Validate and set the backend; raises ValueError for unknown names. 
from geoflow.core import config
config.set_backend("cuda")

docs.title: CRS
docs.text:
CRS(crs_input: str | int | pyproj.CRS | None = "EPSG:4326")

Thin wrapper around pyproj.CRS. Accepts anything pyproj.CRS.from_user_input accepts ("EPSG:32646", 32646, WKT, PROJ strings). None resolves to EPSG:4326.

Member Returns Description pyproj_crs pyproj.CRS Underlying object. epsg int \| None EPSG code if one can be determined. is_geographic bool Degrees-based CRS. is_projected bool Projected CRS (usually metres). to_string() str "EPSG:xxxx" when possible, otherwise WKT. == bool Compares against CRS, str, int or pyproj.CRS.

Warning

CRS defines __eq__ without __hash__, so instances cannot be used as dict keys or in sets. Use crs.to_string() as the key instead. str(crs) returns the repr ("CRS('EPSG:4326')"), not "EPSG:4326".

docs.title: reproject_bounds
docs.text:
reproject_bounds(bounds, src_crs, dst_crs) -> (minx, miny, maxx, maxy)

Transforms the four corners of a bounding box and returns their envelope. It returns the input unchanged when both CRSs are equal. Only corners are sampled, so very large boxes in curved projections can be slightly under-estimated.

docs.title: check_crs_compatibility
docs.text:
check_crs_compatibility(crs1, crs2, context: str = "")

Emits a UserWarning (it doesn't raise) when two CRSs differ. Used by Image band math and Geometry set operations.

docs.title: Filter
docs.text:
Filter(predicate_fn: Callable[[Any], bool], description: str = "Filter")

A declarative predicate, modelled on ee.Filter. Filters are callables: f(item) -> bool. They are consumed by ImageCollection.filter, FeatureCollection.filter, filterBounds, filterDate, and so on.

docs.title: How property values are looked up
docs.text:
For a property name, Filter looks in this order:

  1. item[name] if item is a dict
  2. item.properties[name] (e.g. Feature)
  3. item.metadata[name] (e.g. Image)
  4. getattr(item, name) (e.g. a pandas row)
  5. otherwise None

Silent failures

Filter.__call__ catches every exception and returns False. A typo in a property name, or comparing a string to a number, quietly removes all items instead of raising. If a filtered collection is unexpectedly empty, test the filter against one item by hand.

docs.title: Comparison filters
docs.text: Classmethod GEE alias Matches when eq(name, value) equals value == v neq(name, value) notEquals value != v (also matches when the property is missing) gt(name, value) greaterThan v > value (missing → False) gte(name, value) greaterThanOrEquals v >= value lt(name, value) lessThan v < value lte(name, value) lessThanOrEquals v <= value rangeContains(name, lo, hi) – lo <= v <= hi inList(name, values) – v in values notInList(name, values) – v not in values stringContains(name, sub, case_sensitive=True) – substring match (non-strings → False) stringStartsWith(name, prefix) – prefix match stringEndsWith(name, suffix) – suffix match

docs.title: Temporal filters
docs.text:
Classmethod Description date(start, end) Inclusive window. start/end can be str (ISO), date or datetime. Strings are truncated to the date part. calendarRange(start, end, field="month") field is "month" (1–12) or "day_of_year" (1–366). Wraps around the year when start > end (e.g. 11, 2 = Nov–Feb). dayOfYear(start, end) Shortcut for calendarRange(..., field="day_of_year").

The item date is read from the first non-empty of date, datetime, timestamp or time_start (calendarRange skips time_start).

Note

Items without a parseable date pass temporal filters (lenient by design). Compact strings such as "2023001T042149" (HLS) cannot be parsed and therefore always pass.

docs.title: Spatial filters
docs.text: Classmethod Description bounds(geometry) / intersects(geometry) geometry can be a Geometry, a Shapely geometry or a [minx, miny, maxx, maxy] list. Uses item.geometry if present, otherwise box(*item.bounds). No CRS reprojection is done. Items with no geometry pass.

docs.title: Boolean combinators
docs.text:
Form Equivalent Filter.and_(f1, f2, ...) f1 & f2 Filter.or_(f1, f2, ...) f1 \| f2 Filter.not_(f) ~f 
f = (gf.Filter.eq("platform", "Sentinel-2A")
     & gf.Filter.date("2023-01-01", "2023-06-30")
     & ~gf.Filter.gt("cloud_cover", 20))
f({"platform": "Sentinel-2A", "date": "2023-03-15", "cloud_cover": 5})  # True

docs.title: Reducer
docs.text:
Reducer(name: str, fn: Callable[[np.ndarray, int | None], Any], params: dict | None = None)

Wraps an aggregation function. reducer.reduce(data, axis=None) calls fn(data, axis). Built-in reducers ignore NaN.

Factory Output for axis=None Notes Reducer.mean() scalar np.nanmean Reducer.median() scalar np.nanmedian Reducer.min() / max() scalar np.nanmin / np.nanmax Reducer.sum() scalar np.nansum Reducer.stdDev() scalar population std (ddof=0) Reducer.variance() scalar population variance Reducer.count() int number of non-NaN values Reducer.mode() scalar scipy.stats.mode(nan_policy="omit") Reducer.percentile(p) array of len(p) p is a number or list Reducer.minMax() (min, max) tuple Reducer.histogram(bins=50) {"counts": [...], "edges": [...]} always flattens and ignores axis Reducer.first() / last() element no NaN skipping

Collection compositing

ImageCollection composites only work with reducers that return one value per pixel (mean, median, min, max, sum, stdDev, variance, count, mode, first, last). percentile, minMax and histogram change the output shape and fail.

docs.title: Custom reducers
docs.text:
iqr = gf.Reducer("iqr", lambda a, ax: np.nanpercentile(a, 75, axis=ax) - np.nanpercentile(a, 25, axis=ax))
img.reduceRegion(iqr, geometry=aoi)

docs.title: Earthdata & Datasets API Reference (geoflow.earthdata, geoflow.auth, geoflow.datasets)
docs.text:
GeoFlow provides integrated pipelines for NASA Earthdata authentication, CMR discovery, parallel downloading, cloud-native STAC streaming, and mission-specific adapters such as NASA GEDI LiDAR.

Module Purpose geoflow.auth NASA Earthdata Login session management geoflow.earthdata.search Common Metadata Repository (CMR) granule queries geoflow.earthdata.downloader Multi-threaded download engine with resume & caching geoflow.earthdata.stac Direct raster streaming from AWS & Planetary Computer geoflow.datasets.gedi NASA GEDI Level-2A, 2B, and 4A footprint parser

docs.title: Authentication (geoflow.auth)
docs.text:
from geoflow.auth import login, logout, get_session, is_authenticated, get_s3_credentials

Handles NASA Earthdata Login authentication required to download data from DAACs (LP DAAC, ORNL DAAC, NSIDC, etc.) and in-region AWS S3 cloud direct access.

Function Signature Description login login(strategy: str = "interactive", persist: bool = True) -> bool Authenticates with Earthdata. Priority: (1) earthaccess backend, (2) EARTHDATA_USERNAME / EARTHDATA_PASSWORD env vars, (3) ~/.netrc (or ~/_netrc on Windows), (4) Interactive terminal / Colab prompt. logout logout() -> None Clears active in-memory session. get_session get_session() -> Any Returns active session object or credential dict. is_authenticated is_authenticated() -> bool Returns True if active session is authenticated. get_s3_credentials get_s3_credentials(daac: str = "LPDAAC") -> dict Obtains temporary direct AWS S3 credentials for in-region NASA DAAC buckets (us-west-2) for zero-egress cloud streaming. 
import geoflow as gf

# Login interactively or via .netrc
gf.auth.login(strategy="interactive")
print(f"Authenticated: {gf.auth.is_authenticated()}")

# In AWS us-west-2 cloud:
s3_creds = gf.auth.get_s3_credentials("LPDAAC")

docs.text:
GeoFlow maps user-friendly names to official NASA DAAC short names via DATASET_SHORTNAMES:

Alias NASA CMR Short Name Sensor / Description "SENTINEL-2" HLSS30 Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (Sentinel-2 MSI, 30m) "LANDSAT-8" HLSL30 Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (Landsat-8/9 OLI, 30m) "GEDI/L2A" GEDI02_A GEDI Elevation & Height Metrics (25m footprint) "GEDI/L2B" GEDI02_B GEDI Canopy Cover & Vertical Profile Metrics "GEDI/L4A" GEDI04_A GEDI Aboveground Biomass Density (AGBD) "MODIS" MOD09GA MODIS Surface Reflectance Daily L2G "NASADEM" NASADEM_HGT NASA DEM Global 1 arc second (~30m) 
aoi = gf.Rectangle([91.7, 22.2, 92.0, 22.5])
granules = gf.earthdata.search(
    dataset="SENTINEL-2",
    region=aoi,
    start="2023-01-01",
    end="2023-01-31",
    cloud_cover=20.0,
    limit=5
)
for g in granules:
    print(g["title"], g["time_start"])

docs.title: Resilient Downloader (geoflow.earthdata.downloader)
docs.text:
from geoflow.earthdata import download

Downloads granules in parallel with disk checks and resume support.

download(
    granules: list[dict[str, Any]] | list[str] | Any,
    output_dir: str | Path = "./data",
    workers: int = 4,
    resume: bool = True,
    cache: bool = True
) -> list[Path]

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Disk Space Pre-check: Verifies target volume has at least 500 MB free via check_disk_space().
  • Parallel Threads: Downloads files concurrently via Python's ThreadPoolExecutor.
  • Chunked Resumption: Writes .part temporary files and uses HTTP Range headers to resume interrupted downloads.
  • Caching: If a destination file already exists and has non-zero size, it is retained without re-downloading.

docs.title: Cloud-Native STAC Streaming (geoflow.earthdata.stac)
docs.text:

Allows analysis of cloud-optimized rasters (COG / Zarr) stored in AWS Open Data and Microsoft Planetary Computer without downloading gigabytes of raw data.

Uses odc.stac to load cloud assets into lazy, Dask-backed xarray slices and wraps them into a GeoFlow ImageCollection.

docs.title: GEDI LiDAR Adapter (geoflow.datasets.gedi)
docs.text:
gf.GEDI(
    level: str = "L2A",
    files: list[str] | None = None,
    metadata: dict[str, Any] | None = None
)

Specialized adapter for NASA Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) spaceborne waveform LiDAR data.

Use GEDI.load() to get data

gf.GEDI("L2A") on its own has no data files: its filters only apply to files you already have. Call gf.GEDI.load(...) to search NASA and download granules (this needs an Earthdata login), or pass files=[...] with .h5 files you downloaded before. GEDI granules are large (often more than 1 GB each), so start with a small limit.

gedi = gf.GEDI.load("L2A", region=aoi, start="2022-01-01", end="2022-03-31", limit=1)
gdf = gedi.filterQuality().select(["rh98", "sensitivity"]).to_geodataframe()

docs.text:
GEDI.load(
    level: str = "L2A",

Executes search_data, downloads the resulting HDF5 (.h5) files, and returns an initialized GEDI instance with active bounding box and date filters.

docs.title: Pipeline Methods
docs.text: Method Description .filterBounds(aoi) Filters shots to bounding box of aoi. .filterDate(start, end) Sets temporal filter bounds. .filterQuality() Activates quality mask: retains quality_flag == 1, degrade_flag == 0, and sensitivity >= 0.90. .select(variables) Selects metrics to extract (e.g. ["rh98", "rh50", "sensitivity", "agbd"]). .to_geodataframe() Parses live HDF5 files using h5py across all laser beams (BEAM0000, BEAM0001, etc.) and extracts georeferenced point footprints into a GeoDataFrame. .to_feature_collection() (alias: .to_fc()) Wraps the extracted footprint points into a FeatureCollection.

docs.title: Extracted Footprint Columns
docs.text:
When parsing HDF5 files or working with GEDI point collections: - shot_number: Unique 64-bit laser shot ID. - beam: Laser beam identifier (e.g., "BEAM0101"). - latitude, longitude, elevation: Ground return position. - quality_flag, sensitivity: Signal quality indicators. - rh50, rh98, rh100: Relative height percentiles (canopy top height). - agbd: Aboveground Biomass Density in $Mg / ha$ (for Level-4A). - geometry: shapely.geometry.Point(longitude, latitude).

.select() keeps only the variables you list, plus latitude, longitude and geometry. Include shot_number or beam in the list if you need them.

No files, no data

.to_geodataframe() raises a ValueError on a GEDI object without files, and returns an empty GeoDataFrame (with a warning) when no shots pass the region, date and quality filters. GeoFlow never invents synthetic shots.

docs.title: Machine Learning, Validation & Sampling API Reference (geoflow.validation, geoflow.ml, geoflow.sampling)
docs.text:
Geospatial machine learning models frequently suffer from severe over-optimistic evaluation due to spatial autocorrelation between adjacent training and validation samples. GeoFlow provides spatial cross-validation splitters, spatial buffer dead-zones, automated data leakage diagnostics, spatial error diagnostics, and patch dataset generators for deep learning.

Module Source Files Purpose geoflow.validation spatial_cv.py, leakage.py, diagnostics.py Spatial blocked CV, buffered exclusion zones, leakage audits, and residual Moran's I diagnostics geoflow.ml datasets.py Geospatial patch extraction for CNNs, ViTs, PyTorch DataLoader, and NumPy pipelines geoflow.sampling spatial_sampling.py Stratified point sampling, minimum distance dispersion, and Clark-Evans clustering reports

docs.title: Validation (geoflow.validation)
docs.text: import geoflow.validation as val

docs.title: Spatially Blocked Cross-Validation (SpatialCV)
docs.text:
cv = gf.validation.SpatialCV(
    blocks: FeatureCollection | gpd.GeoDataFrame | int = 5,
    n_splits: int = 5,
    shuffle: bool = True,
    random_state: int = 42
)

Partitions observations such that points located within the same spatial polygon block are never split across training and validation partitions.

  • Block Assignment:
  • If blocks is a FeatureCollection or GeoDataFrame, performs a spatial join (sjoin) to assign points to block IDs.
  • If blocks is an int, clusters coordinates into $k$ geographic spatial groups using $k$-means clustering.
  • Methods:
  • split(data, y=None, groups=None) -> Iterator[Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]]: Yields (train_indices, val_indices) arrays.
  • get_n_splits() -> int: Returns n_splits.

docs.title: Buffered Spatial Cross-Validation (BufferedSpatialCV)
docs.text:
cv = gf.validation.BufferedSpatialCV(
    buffer_distance: float = 1000.0,
    n_splits: int = 5,
    blocks: FeatureCollection | gpd.GeoDataFrame | None = None,
    random_state: int = 42,
    unit: str = "meters"   # or "crs" to buffer in the data's own CRS units
)

Enforces a spatial "dead-zone" exclusion buffer around validation blocks. Any training sample that falls within buffer_distance of any validation point is discarded from that fold's training set, eradicating spatial leakage.

# Create spatial blocks in meters
blocks = gf.spatial.block(aoi, size=5000, unit="meters", shape="hexagonal")

# Set up 2000m buffer zone between train and test
cv = gf.validation.BufferedSpatialCV(buffer_distance=2000.0, blocks=blocks, n_splits=5)

for train_idx, val_idx in cv.split(samples_gdf):
    train_data = samples_gdf.iloc[train_idx]
    val_data = samples_gdf.iloc[val_idx]
    # Train scikit-learn or PyTorch model

Coordinate Units Notice

With the default unit="meters", buffer_distance is in metres. Data in a geographic CRS (e.g. EPSG:4326) is projected to its local UTM zone for buffering, so the buffer is correct at any latitude. Pass unit="crs" to buffer in the dataset's own CRS units instead.

docs.title: Spatial Leakage Diagnostics (leakage_report)
docs.text:
report = gf.validation.leakage_report(
    train: Any,
    test: Any,
    buffer_threshold: float = 0.0,
    unit: str = "meters"
) -> LeakageReport

Audits two partitions (training vs validation, or train vs test) for duplicate locations and proximity violations. Distances are in metres (geographic data is projected to its local UTM zone); pass unit="crs" for CRS units. Set buffer_threshold to the range of spatial autocorrelation: with the default 0.0 proximity is not checked.

docs.title: LeakageReport
docs.text:
• .has_leakage (bool): True if duplicate locations exist or min_distance < buffer_threshold.
  • .has_overlap (bool): Convex hulls of train and test intersect. Informational only: interleaved spatial blocks always overlap at hull level without leaking.
  • .proximity_checked (bool): True when a buffer_threshold > 0 was given.
  • .duplicate_count (int): Count of samples sharing identical coordinates ($< 10^{-7}$ separation).
  • .min_distance (float): Euclidean distance between closest train and test sample points.
  • .buffer_violation (bool): True if min_distance < buffer_threshold.
  • .train_count, .test_count: Sample sizes.
  • .summary() (str): Multi-line diagnostic report and recommendations.

docs.title: Spatial Model Diagnostics (evaluate_spatial)
docs.text:
report = gf.validation.evaluate_spatial(
    y_true: np.ndarray | list[float],
    y_pred: np.ndarray | list[float],
    geometry: Any | None = None,
    k: int = 8
) -> SpatialEvalReport

Evaluates regression predictions using standard numerical metrics alongside Residual Moran's I to detect whether model errors cluster geographically.

docs.title: SpatialEvalReport
docs.text:
• .rmse: Root Mean Squared Error.
  • .mae: Mean Absolute Error.
  • .r2: Coefficient of determination ($R^2$).
  • .residuals: 1D array of residuals ($y_{\text{true}} - y_{\text{pred}}$).
  • .moran: MoranResult of the residuals (tests if errors violate independence).
  • .summary(): Diagnostic readout interpreting whether the model suffers from omitted spatial covariates.
  • .residual_map(ax=None) (alias: .error_map): Plots residuals spatially on Matplotlib axes with a diverging colormap.

docs.title: Machine Learning & Patch Datasets (geoflow.ml)
docs.text: from geoflow.ml import PatchDataset

docs.title: PatchDataset
docs.text:
dataset = gf.ml.PatchDataset(
    image: Image,
    labels: Image | str | np.ndarray | None = None,
    region: Geometry | None = None,
    patch_size: int = 64,
    stride: int = 32,
    transform: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = None,
    metadata: dict[str, Any] | None = None
)

Extracts 2D/3D spatial image patches from multi-band rasters, tracking georeferenced bounding boxes and handling continuous or categorical raster labels.

  • Filters out patches with $> 80\%$ nan or missing pixels.
  • Indexing dataset[i] returns patch_x of shape (bands, patch_size, patch_size) or (patch_x, patch_y).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
• .to_geodataframe() -> gpd.GeoDataFrame: Returns polygon footprint geometries for each patch.
  • .split(strategy="spatial", blocks=None, buffer_distance=0.0, ratios=(0.7, 0.15, 0.15), block_size=None, random_state=42): Splits the patch dataset into (train_ds, val_ds, test_ds).
  • strategy="spatial" assigns whole blocks to a subset: the given blocks polygons, or square blocks of block_size pixels (default 2 * patch_size). strategy="random" assigns individual patches.
  • With either strategy, train patches whose pixel window overlaps (or lies within buffer_distance CRS units of) a val/test patch are dropped, and val patches overlapping test patches are dropped, so subsets never share pixels even when stride < patch_size. A warning is issued if more than 25% of patches are dropped.
  • .dataloader(batch_size=32, shuffle=True, device="cpu"):
  • If PyTorch is installed, returns a native torch.utils.data.DataLoader yielding float32 tensors with pinned memory.
  • If PyTorch is not installed, returns a pure NumPy batch iterator yielding stacked mini-batch arrays.
import geoflow as gf

img = gf.Image("sentinel2_rgbnir.tif")
dataset = gf.ml.PatchDataset(img, patch_size=128, stride=64)

# Create PyTorch-compatible batch generator
train_loader = dataset.dataloader(batch_size=16, shuffle=True)
for batch in train_loader:
    # batch shape: (16, 4, 128, 128)
    pass

docs.title: Sampling Spatial Bias Diagnostics (bias_report)
docs.text:
bias_report(samples: FeatureCollection | gpd.GeoDataFrame) -> dict[str, Any]

Evaluates spatial clustering in field observation coordinates using the Clark-Evans Nearest Neighbor Ratio ($R$): - $R < 1.0$: Spatially clustered distribution (high pseudoreplication risk). - $R \approx 1.0$: Spatially random Poisson process. - $R > 1.0$: Spatially dispersed / regular grid sampling.

Returns a dictionary with "sample_size", "mean_nn_distance", "clark_evans_r", and "spatial_pattern".

docs.text: Property Type Description .data np.ndarray Raw 3D NumPy array of shape (bands, height, width) with float32 dtype. .shape tuple[int, int, int] Dimensions (bands, height, width). .bands list[str] List of band names (e.g. ["B2", "B3", "B4", "B8"]). .count int Number of spectral bands. .height int Height in pixels (rows). .width int Width in pixels (columns). .transform rasterio.Affine Affine geotransform matrix mapping pixel coordinates to CRS space. .crs CRS Coordinate Reference System wrapper. .nodata float Always np.nan: nodata values (and dataset masks) are converted to NaN when an image is loaded or created with nodata=. .bounds tuple[float, float, float, float] Spatial extent as (minx, miny, maxx, maxy). .geometry Geometry Bounding rectangle geometry in the image's CRS.

docs.title: Band Selection & Renaming
docs.text:
Method Description .select(bands, new_names=None) Select one or more bands by string name or integer 0-index. Returns a new Image. Optional new_names renames the selected bands. .rename(new_names) Renames all bands in the current image. Length of new_names must match .count. 
b4_b8 = img.select(["B4", "B8"], new_names=["Red", "NIR"])

docs.title: Band Math & Arithmetic
docs.text:
Arithmetic operations can be performed using native Python operators or method equivalents:

Method Operator Description .add(other) + Pixel-wise addition with a scalar or another Image. .subtract(other) - Pixel-wise subtraction. .multiply(other) * Pixel-wise multiplication. .divide(other) / Safe pixel-wise division (divide-by-zero produces np.nan without crashing). .pow(power) ** Exponentiation. .abs() – Absolute value. .sqrt() – Square root (negative values produce np.nan). .log(), .log10() – Natural logarithm and Base-10 logarithm. .exp() – Exponential function ($e^x$). .sin(), .cos(), .tan() – Trigonometric functions. .floor(), .ceil(), .round() – Rounding functions. __neg__() -img Negates array values.

docs.title: Comparison Operators (Thresholding Masks)
docs.text: Expression Operator Output img > threshold __gt__ 1.0 where true, 0.0 where false img >= threshold __ge__ (alias: __gte__) 1.0 where true, 0.0 where false img < threshold __lt__ 1.0 where true, 0.0 where false img <= threshold __le__ (alias: __lte__) 1.0 where true, 0.0 where false img == other __eq__ 1.0 where true, 0.0 where false img != other __ne__ 1.0 where true, 0.0 where false

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
img.expression(expr_str: str, band_dict: dict[str, Image | float] | None = None) -> Image

Evaluates a mathematical string expression with band variables and mathematical functions (sin, cos, tan, log, exp, sqrt, abs).

# Variables from dictionary or automatically inferred from image band names
custom_index = img.expression(
    "(2.5 * (NIR - RED)) / (NIR + 6.0 * RED - 7.5 * BLUE + 1.0)",
    {"NIR": img.select("B8"), "RED": img.select("B4"), "BLUE": img.select("B2")}
)

docs.title: Spectral Indices
docs.text:
Built-in indices include intelligent auto-detection of common band aliases (e.g., "B8", "B8A", "B08", "NIR", "B4", "B04", "RED", "B3", "B03", "GREEN"):

Method Formula Band Alias Resolution .normalizedDifference([b1, b2]) $(b_1 - b_2) / (b_1 + b_2)$ Required list of 2 band names .ndvi(nir=None, red=None) Normalized Difference Vegetation Index Auto-detects NIR (B8, B8A, B08, NIR) / Red (B4, B04, RED) .ndwi(green=None, nir=None) Normalized Difference Water Index Auto-detects Green (B3, B03, GREEN) / NIR (B8, B8A, B08, NIR) .ndbi(swir=None, nir=None) Normalized Difference Built-Up Index Auto-detects SWIR (B11, SWIR) / NIR (B8, B8A, B08, NIR) .nbr(nir=None, swir2=None) Normalized Burn Ratio Auto-detects NIR (B8, B8A, B08) / SWIR-2 (B12, SWIR2) .evi(nir=None, red=None, blue=None) Enhanced Vegetation Index Auto-detects NIR, Red, Blue .savi(nir=None, red=None, L=0.5) Soil Adjusted Vegetation Index Auto-detects NIR, Red, Canopy factor L

docs.title: Spatial Statistics & Inference API Reference (geoflow.spatial & geoflow.stats)
docs.text:
GeoFlow provides first-class spatial econometrics, geostatistics, and research design inference tools built specifically to detect spatial autocorrelation, model variograms, generate spatial blocking, and calculate Spatial Effective Sample Size (ESS) to prevent pseudoreplication.

Module Source Files Purpose geoflow.spatial autocorrelation.py, local_stats.py, weights.py, blocks.py, variogram.py Spatial weights, Moran's I, LISA clusters, spatial blocking, and semivariograms geoflow.stats inference.py Spatial Effective Sample Size, hypothesis testing with spatial warnings, and power analysis

docs.title: Spatial Weights (SpatialWeights)
docs.text:
from geoflow.spatial import SpatialWeights, knn, distance

Constructs spatial neighborhood weight matrices with automatic row standardization.

Function Signature Description knn knn(data: Any, k: int = 8) -> SpatialWeights Constructs K-Nearest Neighbor spatial weights from point coordinates or polygon centroids. distance distance(data: Any, threshold: float | None = None) -> SpatialWeights Constructs distance-band threshold spatial weights. Defaults to $1.5 \times$ median nearest-neighbor distance.

docs.title: SpatialWeights Class Methods
docs.text:
• .row_standardize() -> SpatialWeights: Scales neighbor weights so that every row sums to $1.0$ ($\sum_j w_{ij} = 1$).
  • .to_dense() -> np.ndarray: Converts sparse dictionary weights into a dense $N \times N$ NumPy matrix.

docs.title: Global Spatial Autocorrelation: Moran's I & Geary's C
docs.text:
moran = gf.spatial.morans_i(data, value="rh98", weights=None, k=8)
c_stat = gf.spatial.gearys_c(data, value="rh98", weights=None, k=8)

docs.title: morans_i
docs.text:
Computes Global Moran's I against an analytical randomization null hypothesis.

  • Parameters:
  • data: A GeoDataFrame or FeatureCollection.
  • value: Attribute column name (or 1D NumPy array).
  • weights: Optional SpatialWeights matrix. If None, builds a $k$-nearest neighbor matrix.
  • k: Neighbor count for automatic KNN weights (default: 8).
  • Returns: A MoranResult object.

docs.title: MoranResult
docs.text:
Encapsulates test statistics and hypothesis evaluation:

Attribute Type Description .I float Observed Global Moran's I statistic ($-1.0$ to $+1.0$). Positive indicates spatial clustering; negative indicates spatial dispersion. .expected float Analytical expected value under spatial randomness: $-1 / (N - 1)$. .variance float Analytical variance under the randomization assumption. .z_score float Standardized test score: $(I - E[I]) / \sqrt{\text{Var}(I)}$. .p_value float Two-tailed $p$-value from standard normal distribution. .n int Sample size. .summary() str Formatted multi-line text report of the statistical test.

Documentation Errata

Older tutorials referenced .p_sim and .z_sim. The true attributes on MoranResult are .p_value and .z_score.

docs.title: Local Spatial Autocorrelation: LISA (local_morans_i)
docs.text:
lisa_gdf = gf.spatial.local_morans_i(data, value, weights=None, k=8, p_threshold=0.05)

Computes Anselin's Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) for each individual spatial observation.

  • Parameters:
  • p_threshold: Alpha level to assign significant clusters (default: 0.05).
  • Returns: A copy of the input GeoDataFrame with 5 newly appended diagnostic columns:
  • value_std: Standardized deviation from the mean ($z_i = y_i - \bar{y}$).
  • I: Local Moran's statistic $I_i$.
  • z_score: Standardized local score.
  • p_value: Local significance $p$-value.
  • cluster: Categorical classification string:
    • "HH": High-High spatial cluster (hotspot: high value surrounded by high values).
    • "LL": Low-Low spatial cluster (coldspot: low value surrounded by low values).
    • "HL": High-Low spatial outlier (high value surrounded by low values).
    • "LH": Low-High spatial outlier (low value surrounded by high values).
    • "not significant": Observation does not deviate from spatial randomness ($p > p_{\text{threshold}}$).

docs.title: Spatial Blocking (block)
docs.text:
blocks = gf.spatial.block(
    aoi: Geometry | Any,
    size: float = 5000.0,
    unit: str = "meters",
    shape: str = "square"  # "square", "grid", or "hexagonal"
) -> FeatureCollection

Partitions an area of interest into spatial blocks to support leakage-safe machine learning cross-validation and spatially stratified sampling.

  • Automatic Metric Reprojection: If aoi is geographic (e.g. EPSG:4326) and unit="meters", block() dynamically determines the local UTM zone, reprojects the geometry to metric coordinates, tessellates the grid, and projects the resulting block boundaries back to the source CRS.
  • Shapes:
  • "square" / "grid": Regular square grid blocks of dimension size x size.
  • "hexagonal": Regular hexagonal tessellation with radius $R = \text{size} / \sqrt{3}$.
  • Output: FeatureCollection containing block_id and polygon geometries.

docs.title: Empirical Semivariograms (variogram)
docs.text:
var_result = gf.spatial.variogram(data, value, n_lags=15, max_dist=None)

Models spatial autocorrelation decay as a function of Euclidean separation distance: $$\gamma(h) = \frac{1}{2 N(h)} \sum_{i=1}^{N(h)} (z(x_i) - z(x_i + h))^2$$

  • Returns: A VariogramResult object.
  • .lag_distances: 1D array of mean bin separation distances $h$.
  • .semivariances: 1D array of semivariances $\gamma(h)$.
  • .npairs: Number of observation pairs falling into each distance bin.
  • .nugget: Estimated measurement noise / micro-scale variance at $h \approx 0$.
  • .sill: Estimated total plateau variance.
  • .plot(ax=None, title="Experimental Semivariogram"): Matplotlib scatter & line plot of the experimental variogram.

docs.title: Spatial Effective Sample Size (effective_sample_size)
docs.text:
ess_info = gf.stats.effective_sample_size(data, value="rh98", geometry=None)

In satellite and GIS datasets, observations violate independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to Tobler's First Law. Traditional statistical tests experience severe Type I error inflation (pseudoreplication).

effective_sample_size adjusts the nominal sample size using the spatial autocorrelation parameter $\rho$: $$N_{\text{eff}} = N \cdot \frac{1 - \rho}{1 + \rho}$$

  • Returns a dict:
  • "nominal_n": Total count of rows ($N$).
  • "effective_n": True number of statistically independent observations ($N_{\text{eff}}$).
  • "morans_i": Observed Moran's I.
  • "p_value": Significance of spatial autocorrelation.
  • "design_effect": Ratio $N / N_{\text{eff}}$.
  • "pseudoreplication_risk": Boolean alert (True when design effect $> 2.0$ and $p < 0.05$).

docs.title: Spatial Hypothesis Testing (test)
docs.text:
result = gf.stats.test(data, value="rh98", group="landcover_class", method=None)

Performs two-sample or multi-sample hypothesis tests with effect sizes and automated spatial autocorrelation alerts.

  • Two Groups:
  • method=None: Welch's $t$-test (robust to unequal variances) with Cohen's $d$ effect size and 95% confidence intervals.
  • method="mann_whitney": Nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test with Rank-Biserial correlation effect size.
  • Three or More Groups:
  • One-way ANOVA with Eta-squared ($\eta^2$) effect size.
  • Spatial Warning: Automatically checks if value exhibits pseudoreplication risk. If detected, appends a warning to result.spatial_warning.

docs.title: StatTestResult
docs.text:
• .test_name: Name of test performed.
  • .statistic: Test statistic ($t$, $U$, or $F$).
  • .p_value: Test $p$-value.
  • .effect_size: Standardized effect size magnitude.
  • .effect_type: "cohens_d", "rank_biserial", or "eta_squared".
  • .ci_95: 95% Confidence interval tuple.
  • .sample_sizes: Dictionary of counts per group.
  • .spatial_warning: Spatial pseudoreplication advisory string (or None).
  • .summary(): Formatted text printout.

Calculates required sample size per experimental group for a two-sample $t$-test given Cohen's $d$ effect size, significance level $\alpha$, and statistical power ($1 - \beta$).

docs.title: NASA Earthdata Login
docs.text:
Some GeoFlow data comes from NASA: GEDI LiDAR (gf.GEDI), HLS Landsat/Sentinel-2 (gf.ImageCollection.from_earthdata) and anything you fetch with gf.search and gf.download. NASA requires a free Earthdata Login account to download it. This page walks you through creating one and connecting it to GeoFlow.

Don't need NASA data yet?

Sentinel-2, Landsat and other imagery from Microsoft Planetary Computer (gf.ImageCollection.from_stac(...)) needs no account at all. The cartography tutorial uses only that.

docs.title: Step 1: Create your Earthdata account
docs.text:
1. Go to https://urs.earthdata.nasa.gov/users/new.
  2. Choose a username and password. You'll type these into GeoFlow later, so write the username down exactly.
  3. Fill in your name, email, country, affiliation and study area, accept NASA's terms and click Register for Earthdata Login.
  4. Open the confirmation email from NASA and click the activation link. Downloads fail until the account is activated.

docs.title: Step 2: Authorize the data centres you'll use
docs.text:
NASA's archives are run by separate data centres (DAACs). Each one has an "application" that must be authorized on your account before it accepts your downloads. If it isn't, downloads fail with HTTP 401 or a 500 error from urs.earthdata.nasa.gov/oauth/authorize.

GeoFlow data Data centre GEDI L2A / L2B (gf.GEDI("L2A"), "L2B") LP DAAC GEDI L4A biomass ORNL DAAC HLS Sentinel-2 / Landsat (from_earthdata("SENTINEL-2")) LP DAAC

The most reliable way to authorize one is to download a single file in your browser:

  1. Sign in at https://urs.earthdata.nasa.gov.
  2. In the same browser, open any data link for that data centre, for example a GEDI file URL from a GeoFlow error message or from a gf.search(...) result.
  3. If NASA shows an Authorize page for the application, approve it. The file then starts downloading, and you can cancel it.

You can review and approve applications any time under Applications → Authorized Apps in your Earthdata profile.

docs.title: Step 3: Log in from GeoFlow
docs.text:
Jupyter / terminalGoogle ColabScripts / servers 
import geoflow as gf

gf.login()  # asks for your Earthdata username and password

GeoFlow saves the credentials to ~/.netrc (_netrc on Windows) so later sessions log in without asking. Use gf.login(persist=False) to keep them in memory only.

Colab forgets files when the runtime restarts, so the safest setup is Colab Secrets:

  1. Click the 🔑 key icon in Colab's left sidebar.
  2. Add a secret named EARTHDATA_USERNAME with your username, and one named EARTHDATA_PASSWORD with your password. Turn on Notebook access for both.
  3. Log in at the top of your notebook:
import os
from google.colab import userdata
import geoflow as gf

os.environ["EARTHDATA_USERNAME"] = userdata.get("EARTHDATA_USERNAME")
os.environ["EARTHDATA_PASSWORD"] = userdata.get("EARTHDATA_PASSWORD")
gf.login()

Your password never appears in the notebook, so you can share it safely. Alternatively, gf.login() on its own prompts for both values.

Set two environment variables before starting Python:

export EARTHDATA_USERNAME="your-username"
export EARTHDATA_PASSWORD="your-password"

Then gf.login() picks them up without prompting.

Keep your password private

Never paste your password into a notebook cell, a script you share, or a GitHub repository. Use the prompt, Colab Secrets or environment variables shown above.

docs.title: Step 4: Check it works
docs.text:
Download one small GEDI granule over your area. GEDI files are large (often more than 1 GB), so always start with limit=1:

aoi = gf.Rectangle([91.76, 22.27, 91.90, 22.40])  # replace with your area

gedi = (
    gf.GEDI("L2A")
    .filterBounds(aoi)
    .filterDate("2022-01-01", "2022-03-31")
    .filterQuality()
    .select(["rh98", "sensitivity"])
    .load(limit=1)
)
gdf = gedi.to_geodataframe()
print(len(gdf), "GEDI shots")

Note

gf.login() returns True as soon as it finds credentials, without contacting NASA. A real download, like the one above, is what confirms your username, password and application authorization are right.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
What you see What it means Fix HTTP 401 / "NASA Earthdata refused access" Wrong username or password, account not activated, or the data centre's app isn't authorized Check the activation email, do Step 2, then gf.login(force=True) and re-enter your details 500 Server Error ... urs.earthdata.nasa.gov/oauth/authorize NASA's login server rejected the request, usually for the same reasons as a 401 Same as above "This GEDI object has no data files yet" You filtered a GEDI object but never downloaded anything Add .load(limit=1) at the end of the chain "GEDI.load() needs a region" No area given, which would download orbits from anywhere on Earth Add .filterBounds(aoi) or pass region=aoi "Got an HTML page instead of data" NASA sent its login page instead of the file Run gf.login() before downloading Login worked before, fails now Password changed, or a typo was saved gf.login(force=True) asks again and replaces the saved entry

To log out of the current Python session, call gf.logout(). To remove saved credentials, delete the machine urs.earthdata.nasa.gov line from ~/.netrc.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Welcome to GeoFlow! This guide will get you up and running with the core concepts.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
GeoFlow requires Python 3.10 or newer.

pip install git+https://github.com/ramiz-moktader/geoflow.git

# Optional: interactive maps, PySAL statistics, STAC, PyTorch and notebook widgets
pip install "geoflow[all] @ git+https://github.com/ramiz-moktader/geoflow.git"

# Optional: earthaccess backend (S3 streaming, open_granule); not part of [all]
pip install "geoflow[earthdata] @ git+https://github.com/ramiz-moktader/geoflow.git"

NASA data (GEDI, Earthdata search and downloads) needs a free Earthdata account. Log in once with gf.login().

Google Colab

Use the plain install and skip earthdata: earthaccess upgrades fsspec, which conflicts with Colab's preinstalled gcsfs. If pip asks you to restart the runtime, use Runtime → Restart session before import geoflow.

!pip install -q git+https://github.com/ramiz-moktader/geoflow.git

docs.title: First Steps
docs.text: GeoFlow's syntax is inspired by Google Earth Engine (GEE). You can chain operations seamlessly.

docs.title: Working with Collections
docs.text:
import geoflow as gf

# Define an Area of Interest
aoi = gf.Rectangle([91.7, 22.2, 92.0, 22.5], crs="EPSG:4326")

# Load Sentinel-2 from Microsoft Planetary Computer (free, no account needed)
collection = gf.ImageCollection.from_stac(
    "sentinel-2-l2a",
    geometry=aoi,
    start="2024-01-01",
    end="2024-02-29",
    bands=["B02", "B03", "B04", "B08", "SCL"],
    resolution=20,  # pixel size in metres
)

# Mask clouds and create a composite image
median_img = collection.mask_clouds().median().clip(aoi)

# Calculate a Vegetation Index
ndvi = median_img.ndvi()

docs.title: Authenticating and Downloading NASA Earthdata
docs.text:
GeoFlow seamlessly integrates with NASA's earthaccess to let you securely search and download data right to your environment (like Google Colab), completely abstracted behind a GEE-like API:

import geoflow as gf

# 1. Login to NASA Earthdata (prompts for credentials in Colab)
gf.auth.login(strategy="interactive")
aoi = gf.Rectangle([91.7, 22.2, 92.0, 22.5])

# 2. Seamlessly search, download, and load into a GEE-like ImageCollection!
collection = gf.ImageCollection.from_earthdata(
    dataset="SENTINEL-2", 
    region=aoi, 
    start="2023-01-01", 
    end="2023-01-15",
    bands=["B04", "B8A"]
)

# 3. Calculate median composite & NDVI
ndvi = collection.median().ndvi(nir="B8A", red="B04")

# 4. Generate a publication-ready map (saves directly to disk)
ndvi.plot_carto_map(
    cmap="RdYlGn", vmin=-0.2, vmax=0.8,
    title="Vegetation Index (NDVI) of Chattogram",
    colorbar_label="NDVI",
    save_path="./downloads/chattogram_ndvi_map.png"
)

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text:
Unlike GEE, GeoFlow operates locally or on your own clusters, meaning you have full access to standard Python tools like xarray and geopandas.

# Convert to xarray DataArray
da = median_img.to_xarray()

GeoFlow also preserves your custom Python subclasses through method chains:

class MyCustomImage(gf.Image):
    pass

img = MyCustomImage("data.tif")
result = img.ndvi()
assert isinstance(result, MyCustomImage)  # Type is preserved!

docs.title: Images and Collections User Guide
docs.text: GeoFlow brings the ease of Google Earth Engine's declarative image processing to the Python data science ecosystem.

docs.title: gf.Image
docs.text: The Image object is the core raster data structure.

docs.title: Instantiation
docs.text:
You can load an image from a local file, a NumPy array, or an xarray DataArray.

import geoflow as gf

img = gf.Image("sentinel2.tif")

docs.title: Band Math & Indices
docs.text:
Calculations are lazy and chainable.

# Select specific bands
b4 = img.select("B4")
b8 = img.select("B8")

# Basic math
ndvi_manual = (b8 - b4) / (b8 + b4)

# Or use built-in indices
ndvi = img.ndvi(nir="B8", red="B4")

docs.title: Xarray & rioxarray Integration
docs.text:
Unlike GEE, you can effortlessly drop into xarray and rioxarray for advanced multi-dimensional geospatial processing. Spatial attributes (CRS, transform, resolution, nodata) are written to the .rio accessor automatically.

# Convert to xarray.DataArray with rioxarray spatial metadata
da = img.to_xarray()
# da is an xarray.DataArray with dims ('band', 'y', 'x')

# Native rioxarray accessor support:
print(da.rio.crs)       # e.g., EPSG:4326
print(da.rio.bounds())  # (minx, miny, maxx, maxy)

# Perform rioxarray operations (e.g. reproject, clip)
# da_utm = da.rio.reproject("EPSG:32646")

# Convert back to a GeoFlow Image
processed_img = gf.Image.from_xarray(da)

docs.title: gf.ImageCollection
docs.text: An ImageCollection handles stacks of images (spatiotemporal datacubes).

docs.title: Filtering
docs.text:
You can filter large collections dynamically before processing.

# Load a collection from a STAC catalogue, then narrow it down further
collection = (
    gf.ImageCollection.from_stac(
        "landsat-c2-l2", geometry=aoi, start="2020-01-01", end="2020-12-31",
        bands=["red", "green", "blue", "nir08"], resolution=30,
    )
    .filterBounds(aoi)
    .filterDate("2020-03-01", "2020-05-31")
)

docs.title: Compositing and Temporal Reduction
docs.text:
Combine timeseries of images into single composite images.

# Compute the median pixel value over time
median_composite = collection.median()

# Create a cloud-free mosaic using a quality band
quality_mosaic = collection.qualityMosaic("NDVI")

docs.title: 4D Datacubes
docs.text:
You can convert an entire collection into a 4-dimensional xarray.DataArray (time, band, y, x).

cube = collection.to_xarray()

docs.title: Spatial Statistics User Guide
docs.text: GeoFlow brings advanced spatial statistics directly into the geospatial processing pipeline, bridging the gap between raw data manipulation and spatial econometrics/ecology.

docs.title: Spatial Autocorrelation
docs.text: Spatial autocorrelation measures the degree to which a set of spatial features and their associated data values tend to be clustered together in space.

docs.title: Global Moran's I
docs.text:
Global Moran's I indicates the overall clustering of data in your study area.

import geoflow as gf

# GEDI canopy heights for the area (needs gf.login(); see the Earthdata login guide)
gedi_features = (
    gf.GEDI("L2A").filterBounds(aoi).filterDate("2022-01-01", "2022-03-31")
    .filterQuality().load(limit=1).to_geodataframe()
)

moran = gf.spatial.morans_i(gedi_features, value="rh98", k=8)
print(f"Moran's I: {moran.I:.4f}, p-value: {moran.p_value:.4f}")
print(moran.summary())

docs.title: Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA)
docs.text:
LISA calculates the local Moran's I for each individual feature, identifying spatial clusters (HH, LL) and spatial outliers (HL, LH).

lisa_df = gf.spatial.local_morans_i(gedi_features, value="rh98", k=8)
# lisa_df now contains a 'cluster' column you can use for mapping
print(lisa_df['cluster'].value_counts())

docs.title: Spatial Effective Sample Size (ESS)
docs.text:
When samples are spatially autocorrelated (Tobler's First Law), traditional statistical tests assume independent observations, which leads to artificially low p-values (pseudoreplication).

GeoFlow can calculate the Spatial Effective Sample Size to determine the true number of independent samples you actually have.

ess = gf.stats.effective_sample_size(gedi_features, value="rh98")
print(f"Nominal N: {ess['nominal_n']}")
print(f"Effective N: {ess['effective_n']}")
print(f"Design Effect: {ess['design_effect']:.2f}")
print(f"Pseudoreplication Alert: {ess['pseudoreplication_risk']}")
You can use this reduced N when performing ANOVA or t-tests to avoid Type I errors.

docs.title: Machine Learning and Validation User Guide
docs.text: GeoFlow is built to safely interface with machine learning frameworks like scikit-learn and PyTorch while rigorously protecting against spatial data leakage.

docs.title: The Problem: Spatial Data Leakage
docs.text: In spatial datasets, nearby samples are highly correlated. If you randomly split points into a training set and a validation set, you will likely have validation points that are just a few meters away from training points. Your model will "memorize" the local spatial structure rather than learning generalizable features, leading to severely over-optimistic performance metrics.

docs.title: Solution: Spatial Blocking & Buffered Cross-Validation
docs.text: GeoFlow solves this with Spatial Blocking and Buffered Spatial Cross Validation.

docs.title: 1. Create Spatial Blocks
docs.text:
First, divide your study area into spatial blocks (squares or hexagons).

import geoflow as gf

aoi = gf.Rectangle([91.7, 22.2, 92.0, 22.5])
blocks = gf.spatial.block(aoi, size=5000, unit="meters", shape="hexagonal")

docs.title: 2. Buffered Spatial CV
docs.text:
Next, use BufferedSpatialCV. This splitter ensures that an entire block is held out for validation, AND it enforces a "dead-zone" buffer between the training data and validation block so no training data is physically adjacent to the validation data.

cv = gf.validation.BufferedSpatialCV(
    buffer_distance=2000, # 2km dead-zone
    blocks=blocks,
    n_splits=5
)

for train_idx, val_idx in cv.split(samples_gdf):
    train_data = samples_gdf.iloc[train_idx]
    val_data = samples_gdf.iloc[val_idx]
    # Train your model here...

docs.title: 3. Leakage Diagnostics
docs.text:
You can audit any split using the leakage_report tool:

report = gf.validation.leakage_report(train_data, val_data, buffer_threshold=2000)
print(report.summary())

docs.title: Deep Learning with PyTorch
docs.text:
GeoFlow provides a native PatchDataset that acts as a bridge to deep learning frameworks by generating spatial image patches.

# Create a patch generator from a GeoFlow Image
dataset = gf.ml.PatchDataset(
    image=img,
    patch_size=64, # 64x64 pixel patches
    stride=32      # Overlapping patches
)

# Convert to a PyTorch DataLoader
train_loader = dataset.dataloader(batch_size=32, shuffle=True)

for batch in train_loader:
    # batch is a tensor of shape (32, bands, 64, 64)
    # Feed to your CNN / ViT
    pass

docs.title: Cartography and Visualization
docs.text:
GeoFlow provides tools to generate professional, publication-ready cartographic maps in a single line of code.

New to GeoFlow maps?

Follow the step-by-step cartography tutorial: it builds seven maps from free Sentinel-2 data, with every result shown.

docs.title: Plotting Maps
docs.text:
The plot_map() method handles scaling, North Arrows, Scale Bars, and complex graticule formatting.

import geoflow as gf

img = gf.Image("data.tif")

ax = img.plot_map(
    bands=["B4", "B3", "B2"], # True color composite
    title="Study Area",
    north_arrow=True,
    scale_bar=True,
    grid=True,
    save_path="map.png"
)

docs.title: Graticule and Corner Collision Pruning
docs.text: When plotting maps, coordinates at the corners of the bounding box often collide (e.g., the lowest latitude label overlapping the leftmost longitude label). GeoFlow automatically handles this using cartographic best practices.

docs.title: Four-Sided Graticules and Vertical Latitudes
docs.text:
You can enable coordinate ticks on all four sides and rotate the latitude labels vertically:

img.ndvi().plot_map(
    cmap="RdYlGn",
    title="Vegetation Index",
    show_top=True,
    show_right=True,
    show_bottom=True,
    show_left=True,
    lat_orientation="vertical", # Rotates latitude labels 90°
    prune_corners=True,         # Automatically hides colliding corner labels
    degree_precision=3
)
  • prune_corners: Set to True (default) to suppress corner labels that collide. You can also specify "x", "y", or "both" to enforce which axes have corner labels pruned.
  • lat_orientation: Use "vertical" to align latitude text cleanly alongside the left/right neatlines.
  • tick_fontfamily and tick_fontsize: Style the coordinates for publication (e.g., tick_fontfamily="serif").

docs.title: Interactive Layout Editor (ArcGIS View in Notebooks)
docs.text:
GeoFlow provides an in-notebook layout designer similar to the Print Layout view in ArcGIS Pro or QGIS. It runs directly inside Google Colab, JupyterLab, and VS Code:

# Launch the interactive Layout Editor
editor = img.ndvi().edit_layout(
    title="Study Area — NDVI",
    subtitle="Sentinel-2 MSI Level-2A",
    cmap="RdYlGn",
)

# Display the editor widget in notebook
editor

docs.title: What You Can Customize Interactively:
docs.text:
• 📄 Canvas: Choose standard print sizes (Square, Landscape, Nature Single/Double Column) and custom titles.
  • 🧭 Carto: Toggle & reposition the North Arrow and dynamically scaled metric Scale Bar.
  • 🌐 Graticule: Control 4-sided coordinate labels, vertical/horizontal orientations, decimal precision, and grid styles.
  • 🎨 Colors: Switch between 15+ remote sensing palettes, continuous colorbars, and stretch limits.
  • 💾 Export: Export directly to 300 / 600 DPI, trigger a 1-click Google Colab download, or auto-generate the exact Python code snippet.

docs.title: Interactive Leaflet Maps
docs.text:
For web tile exploratory analysis, use the interactive Map class:

m = gf.Map()
m.centerObject(aoi)
m.addLayer(img, {"bands": ["B4", "B3", "B2"], "min": 0, "max": 3000}, "Sentinel-2")
m.save("interactive.html")

docs.title: Comprehensive End-to-End Tutorial: Remote Sensing, Spatial Statistics & Spatial ML
docs.text:
This tutorial guides you through a complete, rigorous scientific research workflow in GeoFlow (gf).

We will model forest canopy height using spaceborne NASA GEDI LiDAR, multi-spectral Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, rigorous spatial statistics to prevent pseudoreplication, and leakage-safe spatial machine learning with publication-quality cartography.

docs.title: Tutorial Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    AOI[1. Define AOI & Validate CRS] --> Earthdata[2. NASA Earthdata Ingestion]
    Earthdata --> Optical[Sentinel-2 Optical Compositing]
    Earthdata --> LiDAR[GEDI L2A LiDAR Processing]
    Optical --> Sample[3. Point-to-Raster Sampling]
    LiDAR --> Sample
    Sample --> ESDA[4. Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis]
    ESDA --> Moran[Global Moran's I & Geary's C]
    ESDA --> LISA[LISA Hotspot/Outlier Mapping]
    ESDA --> Variogram[Experimental Semivariogram]
    ESDA --> ESS[5. Spatial Effective Sample Size]
    ESS --> SpatialML[6. Leakage-Safe Spatial Machine Learning]
    SpatialML --> Block[Spatial Blocking & BufferedSpatialCV]
    SpatialML --> Audit[Data Leakage Audit Report]
    SpatialML --> Eval[7. Spatial Error Diagnostics]
    Optical --> DeepLearning[8. Deep Learning Patch Extraction]
    Optical --> Carto[9. Publication Cartographic Layout]

docs.title: 1. Study Area Setup & Coordinate System Validation
docs.text:
We define a study area in the biodiverse hill forest tract of Southeastern Bangladesh (Chattogram region) using WGS84 coordinates:

import geoflow as gf

# 1. Define Area of Interest (AOI) bounding box [minx, miny, maxx, maxy]
aoi = gf.Rectangle([91.7, 22.2, 92.0, 22.5], crs="EPSG:4326")

print(f"AOI Extent: {aoi.bounds}")
print(f"Area in sq degrees: {aoi.area:.4f}")
print(f"Centroid: ({aoi.centroid().shapely.x:.3f}, {aoi.centroid().shapely.y:.3f})")

docs.title: 2. Satellite Data Acquisition: Sentinel-2 & GEDI LiDAR
Step 2A: Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel (HLS) Multi-Spectral Imagery
docs.text:
Search and stream or download cloud-filtered optical satellite imagery:

# Authenticate with NASA Earthdata (interactive prompt or .netrc)
gf.auth.login(strategy="interactive")

# Option A: Ingest and download from NASA Earthdata (Harmonized Sentinel-2)
sentinel_collection = gf.ImageCollection.from_earthdata(
    dataset="SENTINEL-2",
    region=aoi,
    start="2023-01-01",
    end="2023-03-31",
    bands=["B02", "B03", "B04", "B08", "B11", "B12"],
    cloud_cover=(0.0, 15.0),
    limit=5
)

# Option B: Cloud-Native Lazy STAC Streaming (Zero download)
# sentinel_collection = gf.ImageCollection.from_stac(
#     collection="sentinel-2-l2a",
#     catalog="planetary-computer",
#     geometry=aoi,
#     start="2023-01-01",
#     end="2023-03-31",
#     bands=["B02", "B03", "B04", "B08"]
# )

print(f"Acquired {len(sentinel_collection)} optical granules.")

docs.title: Step 2B: Temporal Compositing & Spectral Indices
docs.text:
We reduce the time-series using a pixel-wise median composite and compute vegetation indices:

# Create cloud-free median composite clipped to our study area
composite = (
    sentinel_collection
    .filterBounds(aoi)
    .median()
    .clip(aoi)
)

# Rename to standard band names if using HLS naming conventions
if "B04" in composite.bands:
    composite = composite.rename(["B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11", "B12"])

# Compute vegetation & moisture indices
ndvi = composite.ndvi(nir="B8", red="B4")
ndwi = composite.ndwi(green="B3", nir="B8")

print(f"Composite dimensions: {composite.height} x {composite.width} pixels across {composite.count} bands.")

docs.title: Step 2C: NASA GEDI LiDAR Canopy Height Footprints
docs.text:
Extract 25m footprint canopy top heights ($RH98$) from NASA GEDI Level-2A:

# Download GEDI Level-2A granules over our AOI (needs gf.login(); granules are large)
gedi = (
    gf.GEDI("L2A")
    .filterBounds(aoi)
    .filterDate("2022-01-01", "2022-12-31")
    .filterQuality()  # Retain high-sensitivity, non-degraded shots
    .select(["shot_number", "rh98", "rh50", "sensitivity", "elevation"])
    .load(limit=2)
)

# Convert footprint points to a GeoPandas GeoDataFrame and FeatureCollection
gedi_gdf = gedi.to_geodataframe()
gedi_fc = gedi.to_feature_collection()

print(f"Extracted {len(gedi_gdf)} valid LiDAR shots.")
print(gedi_gdf[["shot_number", "rh98", "sensitivity"]].head())

docs.title: 3. Spatial Intersections & Point-to-Raster Sampling
docs.text:
To train predictive models, we need the multi-spectral reflectance and vegetation index values extracted directly underneath each 25-meter GEDI LiDAR shot:

# Sample multi-band satellite data at each LiDAR footprint location
sampled_fc = gedi_fc.sample_raster(
    image=composite,
    bands=["B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11", "B12"]
)

# Also append NDVI to the attribute table
sampled_fc = sampled_fc.sample_raster(image=ndvi, bands=["NDVI"])

# Convert to a standard Pandas DataFrame for statistical modeling
df = sampled_fc.to_dataframe()
print(df[["shot_number", "rh98", "NDVI", "B8", "B4"]].dropna().head())

docs.title: 4. Exploratory Spatial Data Analysis (ESDA)
docs.text: Before fitting any machine learning model, we must test for spatial autocorrelation. Nearby forest plots are not independent; treating them as i.i.d. causes false confidence.

docs.title: Global Moran's I & Geary's C
docs.text:
# Compute Global Moran's I using an 8-nearest neighbor spatial weights matrix
moran = gf.spatial.morans_i(sampled_fc, value="rh98", k=8)
print(moran.summary())

# Compute Geary's C
geary = gf.spatial.gearys_c(sampled_fc, value="rh98", k=8)
print(f"Geary's C: {geary:.4f}")

If $p < 0.05$ and $I > 0$, our canopy height observations exhibit statistically significant spatial clustering.

docs.title: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA Clusters)
docs.text:
Identify local hotspots (High-High), coldspots (Low-Low), and spatial outliers (High-Low, Low-High):

# Compute LISA statistics
lisa_gdf = gf.spatial.local_morans_i(sampled_fc, value="rh98", k=8, p_threshold=0.05)

# Review cluster distribution
print("LISA Spatial Clusters:")
print(lisa_gdf["cluster"].value_counts())

docs.title: Empirical Semivariogram Modeling
docs.text:
Model the distance over which canopy height remains autocorrelated:

# Calculate semivariogram out to 15 distance lags
variogram = gf.spatial.variogram(sampled_fc, value="rh98", n_lags=15)

print(f"Estimated Nugget variance: {variogram.nugget:.3f}")
print(f"Estimated Sill plateau   : {variogram.sill:.3f}")

# Plot experimental semivariogram
ax = variogram.plot(title="Canopy Height Spatial Dependence (Semivariogram)")

docs.title: 5. Preventing Pseudoreplication with Spatial Effective Sample Size (ESS)
docs.text:
When sample points are autocorrelated, sample size is deceptively large. GeoFlow calculates the Effective Sample Size ($N_{\text{eff}}$):

ess_report = gf.stats.effective_sample_size(sampled_fc, value="rh98")

print(f"Nominal Sample Count (N)  : {ess_report['nominal_n']}")
print(f"Effective Sample Size (N_eff): {ess_report['effective_n']}")
print(f"Design Effect (N / N_eff) : {ess_report['design_effect']:.2f}")
print(f"Pseudoreplication Alert   : {ess_report['pseudoreplication_risk']}")

docs.title: Spatial Hypothesis Testing
docs.text:
Test whether canopy heights differ across forest density zones while accounting for spatial autocorrelation:

# Classify points into high vs low vegetation based on NDVI median
median_ndvi = df["NDVI"].median()
df["veg_class"] = (df["NDVI"] > median_ndvi).map({True: "Dense", False: "Sparse"})

# Run hypothesis test with automated spatial autocorrelation alerts
stat_test = gf.stats.test(df, value="rh98", group="veg_class")
print(stat_test.summary())

docs.title: The Trap: Random Train/Test Splits
docs.text: If you use standard train_test_split(test_size=0.2), validation points will sit only meters away from training points. Models "memorize" neighboring pixels rather than generalizable physical features.

docs.title: The Solution: Hexagonal Spatial Blocking & Buffered Spatial CV
docs.text:
# 1. Partition study area into 5 km hexagonal blocks
blocks = gf.spatial.block(aoi, size=5000.0, unit="meters", shape="hexagonal")

# Project samples to local metric coordinates (e.g. UTM) for metric buffers
samples_utm = sampled_fc.gdf.to_crs(blocks.crs.to_string())

# 2. Configure Buffered Spatial Cross-Validation with a 1500m dead-zone
cv = gf.validation.BufferedSpatialCV(
    buffer_distance=1500.0, # 1.5 km spatial exclusion buffer
    blocks=blocks,
    n_splits=5,
    random_state=42
)

# 3. Audit first fold for spatial leakage
train_idx, val_idx = next(cv.split(samples_utm))
train_partition = samples_utm.iloc[train_idx]
val_partition = samples_utm.iloc[val_idx]

audit = gf.validation.leakage_report(
    train=train_partition,
    test=val_partition,
    buffer_threshold=1500.0
)
print(audit.summary())

docs.title: Train and Evaluate a Predictive Model
docs.text:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor

features = ["B2", "B3", "B4", "B8", "B11", "B12", "NDVI"]
target = "rh98"

X_train = train_partition[features].dropna()
y_train = train_partition.loc[X_train.index, target]

X_val = val_partition[features].dropna()
y_val = val_partition.loc[X_val.index, target]

model = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred = model.predict(X_val)

docs.title: 7. Spatial Error Diagnostics (Residual Autocorrelation)
docs.text:
Conventional ML packages only report RMSE and $R^2$. GeoFlow tests the model's residuals for spatial bias:

val_geoms = val_partition.loc[X_val.index, "geometry"]

eval_report = gf.validation.evaluate_spatial(
    y_true=y_val,
    y_pred=y_pred,
    geometry=val_geoms,
    k=8
)

print(eval_report.summary())

# Plot residual map to visually inspect spatial bias
eval_report.residual_map()

If the residuals show no significant Moran's I, the model has generalized cleanly across geography without omitting spatial drivers.

docs.title: 8. Deep Learning Patch Extraction (PyTorch Ready)
docs.text:
For convolutional neural networks (U-Net, ResNet, Vision Transformers), GeoFlow extracts multi-channel image patches and returns PyTorch data loaders:

# Create patch dataset: 64x64 pixel windows with stride 32
patch_ds = gf.ml.PatchDataset(
    image=composite,
    patch_size=64,
    stride=32
)

print(f"Total extracted spatial patches: {len(patch_ds)}")

# Split into train, val, test subsets using spatial blocking
train_ds, val_ds, test_ds = patch_ds.split(
    strategy="spatial",
    blocks=blocks,
    ratios=(0.7, 0.15, 0.15)
)

# Generate mini-batch PyTorch DataLoader (or NumPy iterator)
train_loader = train_ds.dataloader(batch_size=16, shuffle=True)

for batch in train_loader:
    # batch shape: (16, bands, 64, 64)
    print(f"Mini-batch tensor shape: {batch.shape}")
    break

docs.title: Standalone Publication Map Export
docs.text:
Generate a 300 DPI publication map featuring a dynamic metric scale bar, 3D North arrow, and 4-sided graticule degree ticks:

ndvi.plot_map(
    cmap="RdYlGn",
    vmin=-0.1,
    vmax=0.85,
    title="Forest Vegetation Index (NDVI) — Chattogram Region",
    subtitle="Sentinel-2 MSI Level-2A | WGS84 Datum",

    # 4-Sided Graticule with Vertical Latitudes
    show_top=True,
    show_right=True,
    show_bottom=True,
    show_left=True,

    # Cartographic elements

)

Launch the ArcGIS-style interactive Layout Editor directly in your Jupyter or Google Colab notebook:
